correctness.rationale: For n>=5 the Kneser distance is 0 for equal probes, 1 for disjoint ground edges, 2 otherwise. For intersecting targets {a,b},{a,c}, the distinguishing probes are exactly ground edges crossing {b,c}, giving two isolates or a K2 component as the only failures. For disjoint targets the distinguishing set consists of the targets and edges leaving their four-point union. If this union is edge-closed, the target partition must be a balanced K2,2 bipartition; after excluding K2 and two isolates, the remaining connected obstruction is P4 or C4 or P3 plus one isolate. The equivalence holds for every n>=5 (including n=5). For G(n,p) at p=(log n+c)/n, factorial moments of isolates yield Poisson(exp(-c)); Cayley spanning tree bounds eliminate order-2/3/4 components, so P(resolve)->exp(-exp(-c))(1+exp(-c)). Monotonicity justifies drifting windows. An independently written direct metric-distance/subset enumerator agreed with component recognition for all 1024 n=5 and 32768 n=6 ground graphs (resolving counts 843 and 31232). The finite check is not the all-n proof.

value.rationale: A complete linear-time recognition criterion for every resolving probe set of KG(n,2) is a structural strengthening of mere metric dimension. It identifies exact smallest obstruction types and changes the random critical-window limit from the connectivity zero-isolate probability to a one-isolate Poisson tail. Both classifications and the sharp threshold are mathematically motivated and independently usable.
